item.title: Zero Knowledge for Free up to Linear Query Bounds: Quasilinear-Size Constant-Query Zero-Knowledge PCPs
item.description: arXiv:2610.29066v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that for all polynomials $T$ and $b$, every relation in NTIME($T$) has a binary PCP with $O(1)$ non-adaptive queries, perfect completeness, soundness error 1/2 and length $(T+b)\cdot(\log(T+b))^{O(1)}$, which is perfect zero knowledge against every adaptive, possibly malicious verifier making at most $b$ queries. This improves the length $\tilde O(T+b^2)$ of Zeilberger, O'Connor, Gur and Spooner (2026), who observed that Dinur's gap amplification preserves zero knowledge. The simulator runs in expected polynomial time (or in strict polynomial time, with a failure symbol or with negligible statistical error). For $b\le T$ the length is $T\cdot\mathrm{polylog}\,T$, the form of the shortest known constant-query PCPs without zero knowledge. Unless NP $\subseteq$ BPP, the dependence on $b$ is optimal up to the polylogarithmic factor for polynomial-time simulators: zero knowledge is free up to linear query bounds. Zero-knowledge interactive oracle proofs achieved length $\tilde O(T+b)$ in 2016-17; we obtain it for PCPs. Gur, O'Connor and Spooner (STOC 2025) asked whether NP has such PCPs of quasilinear length (their Open Problem 1). This paper answers it for every polynomial query bound, with the simulators above in place of a strict polynomial-time perfect simulator. The proofs were developed with extensive AI assistance and have been checked by the authors. We mask the Reed-Solomon proof of proximity of Ben-Sasson and Sudan at every node of its recursion. By a locator lemma, at every node, whatever $k$ of its proof symbols reveal about its input is determined by $O(k)$ input values. We prove it with the coprime-order argument of Bafna and Vyas (2026); our treatment of domain points is new. Dinur's gap amplification gives constant query complexity. The query count and the polylogarithmic exponent are absolute but very large.
item.dc:creator: Inhyuk Park, Chenglin Fan

item.title: Pfaffian Recognition is in coRP
item.description: arXiv:2610.29817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A graph is called Pfaffian if it admits a Pfaffian orientation. The Pfaffian recognition problem asks whether a given graph is Pfaffian. In 1989, Vazirani and Yannakakis showed that this problem is polynomial time equivalent to testing whether a prescribed orientation is Pfaffian, and that the problem belongs to $\mathsf{coNP}$. The complexity of the problem for general graphs has remained open since then. For bipartite graphs, polynomial time recognition algorithms were obtained by Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas in 1999, and independently by McCuaig in 2004. We show that testing whether a given orientation is Pfaffian can be reduced to polynomial identity testing. This gives a randomized polynomial time algorithm for Pfaffian recognition on general graphs, placing the problem in $\mathsf{coRP}$.
item.dc:creator: Priyanshu Pant, Ranveer Singh

item.title: Tight Bounds on the Randomized Communication Complexity of Vector-in-Subspace
item.description: arXiv:2610.30052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the randomized communication complexity of Vector-in-Subspace in $\mathbb R^n$ with error at most $1/3$ is $\Theta(\sqrt n)$. Alice holds a unit vector $u$ and Bob holds an $n/2$-dimensional subspace $H$; they must distinguish $u\in H$ from $u\in H^\perp$. An exact one-way quantum protocol uses $O(\log n)$ qubits, making the problem a geometric example of an exponential quantum advantage over interactive classical communication. Our lower bound matches Raz's $O(\sqrt n)$ upper bound, improves the $\Omega(n^{1/3})$ lower bound of Klartag and Regev, and removes the total-rank restriction in Grupel's $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ result. The proof establishes a Gaussian moment bound over complete rectangle partitions. A complex Gaussian representation yields a vanishing even moment whose cancellation is preserved when averaging over the partition. We control the signed conditional moments around a real center by decomposing conditional Gaussian measures into fixed coordinates and sub-Gaussian components. Combining this estimate with spherical harmonic analysis gives the communication lower bound.
item.dc:creator: Chengu Wang

item.title: Multiplying matrices via polynomials: exposition and barriers
item.description: arXiv:2610.30054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give an exposition of OpenAI's recent proof that the exponent $\omega_\mathbb{C}$ of matrix multiplication over the complex numbers satisfies $\omega_\mathbb{C}\leq9/4$. Our version of the proof gives $\omega_\mathbb{F}\leq9/4$ over every field $\mathbb{F}$. We also treat the rectangular matrix multiplication exponent $\omega_\mathbb{F}(a,b,c)$. Here we have $\omega_\mathbb{F}(1,k,1)=2$ for $0\leq k\leq1/2$ and $\omega_\mathbb{F}(1,k,1)\leq1+k+1/(4k)$ for $k\geq1/2$, and, for real numbers $a\geq b\geq c\geq0$, $\omega_\mathbb{F}(a,b,c)=a+b$ if $c(a+b)\leq ab$ and $\omega_\mathbb{F}(a,b,c)\leq(a+b+c)/2+(ab/c+ac/b+bc/a)/4$ otherwise. Our exposition is in the language of degeneration inequalities among polynomial multiplication tensors and Strassen's asymptotic spectrum duality. We moreover prove an operational barrier (which can be thought of as coming from an operational asymptotic spectrum) showing that the current analysis of all these upper bounds on $\omega_\mathbb{F}$ and $\omega_\mathbb{F}(a,b,c)$ is optimal and that in fact the current degeneration ingredients cannot improve the bounds.
item.dc:creator: Alimzhan Amanov, Maxim van den Berg, Jeroen Zuiddam

item.title: Amplified Pruning and Path Selectors for Deterministic Radio Gossiping
item.description: arXiv:2610.28930v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study deterministic gossiping in unknown strongly connected directed radio networks with $n$ vertices, $m$ arcs, and distinct identifiers in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, where $N=n^{\mathcal O(1)}$. Messages are unrestricted; collision detection is unavailable. Our protocol combines amplified reception certificates, adaptive pruning, and permutation selectors. Each pruning iteration costs $\mathcal O(n\log^2n\log\log n)$ rounds. A two-step quadratic contraction limits each receiver and each class of identical closed in-neighborhoods to $\mathcal O(\log\log n)$ qualifying selections. Under an explicit degree-concentration condition, our protocol takes $\mathcal O(m\log^2n(\log\log n)^2)$ rounds. For directed regular graphs with common in- and out-degree $\Delta$, our strategy achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n\sqrt\Delta,n^2/\Delta\})$, extending the identifier range of Wu and Chrobak and improving their high-degree bound. At completion entry, let $a\ge1$ count original sources not yet credited as globally disseminated. Permutation selectors reduce our balanced completion budget by a factor of $\log^{2/3}(a+1)$ relative to interleaved path selectors. Our geometric protocol attains $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(k^2+n\tau+\min\{u^2,(nu)^{2/3}\})$ for an original path cover of scale $k$, weight $\tau$, and $u$ exceptions. Every graph also admits $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n^{4/3},N+(mn)^{3/5}\})$ rounds. Only $n,N$ are inputs. Within the stated graph classes and identifier ranges, these results answer the polynomial-identifier and average-degree questions of Wu and Chrobak. The unrestricted general-graph cases remain open.
item.dc:creator: Qin Xin

item.title: Optimal R\'enyi and Logarithmic Additive Functional Entropy Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2610.28999v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We characterize the minimax sample complexity of estimating R\'enyi entropy from independent samples on an alphabet of size at most $k$, when the known order $\alpha>1$ may vary with $k$. For every fixed additive accuracy $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$ and success probability $2/3$, we prove matching bounds with constants independent of $k$ and $\alpha$. For $1<\alpha<\log k$, the rate is $\Theta_\varepsilon(\alpha k^{1-1/\alpha}X_\alpha(k,\varepsilon))$, where a monotone scalar inequality defines $X_\alpha$ at noninteger orders. The bounds remain uniform as the order approaches one or an integer, or grows with the alphabet. Integer orders below $\log k$ have rate $\Theta_\varepsilon(\alpha k^{1-1/\alpha})$; orders at least $\log k$ and min-entropy have rate $\Theta_\varepsilon(k\log k)$. We extend the analysis to logarithms of positive additive functionals. For every fixed continuous $f$ satisfying $f(0)=0$, $f(x)>0$ for $x>0$, and $f(x)\sim ax^r$ at zero, with $a>0$ and $r>1$, estimating $-\beta^{-1}\log\sum_i f(p_i)$ at fixed accuracy, for fixed $\beta>0$, has sample complexity $\Theta(k^{1-1/r})$ for integer $r$ and $\Theta(k/\log k)$ otherwise. A replication reduction preserves the sampling experiment and transfers the rates for powers. Smooth flat functions show that regularity alone does not determine the complexity. The upper bound combines polynomial approximation, Gamma count statistics, and an independent pilot, with a global affine correction near order one. The lower bound uses interpolation to construct positive mean-one priors and controls their distinguishability and entropy separation after normalization. Exact count-variance identities and weighted approximation duality connect the two arguments.
item.dc:creator: Arman Adibi, Piotr Krysta

item.title: Dissipation Bounds and Hardness in Globally Asymptotically Stable Quadratic Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.29512v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study worst-case finite-time energy dissipation in quadratic systems with proved global asymptotic stability (GAS). Estimating the maximum retained energy fraction to any fixed positive additive error below $1/2$ is NP-hard, even when the input includes a strict quartic Lyapunov function and proof of strictness, both constructed in polynomial time. NP denotes nondeterministic polynomial time. For a partially damped family, the unit-sphere minimum norm of the coupling map equals the structured coefficient distance to loss of GAS. Positive distances at most $1/2$ give two-sided inverse-square halving-time bounds with explicit coefficient factors. Polynomial-factor approximation of the least dissipated fraction, halving time or coefficient distance is NP-hard. Additive hardness persists throughout an explicit coefficient neighborhood and under direct damping with exponential stability, a strict quadratic Lyapunov function and a Hurwitz Jacobian. Unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, where P denotes deterministic polynomial time, no polynomial-time algorithm attains these guarantees on all inputs.
item.dc:creator: Subhransu S. Bhattacharjee

item.title: A Quasipolynomial Algorithm for $\ell_\infty$ Contractions
item.description: arXiv:2610.30122v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give an algorithm for computing an $\eps$-approximate fixed point of any $d$-dimensional nonexpansion with respect to the $\ell_\infty$ norm in time $\log(1/\eps)^{O(\log^2 d)}$. At its core, our method uses a boosting argument to geometrically shrink a search region. Among other consequences, our algorithm implies that simple stochastic games can be solved in quasipolynomial time.
item.dc:creator: Ashkan Soleymani, Gabriele Farina

item.title: Temporal Exploration and Rendezvous via Weisfeiler-Leman Colorings
item.description: arXiv:2610.30123v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Temporal graphs are graphs whose edge relation changes in discrete time steps. The Temporal Exploration Problem (TEXP) asks for a temporal walk that visits all vertices. We show that every connected temporal graph with $n$ vertices can be explored in $O(qn\log^3(n))$ time steps, where $q$ is the number of vertex color classes induced by the 2-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (2-WL) coloring. For small $q$, our bound substantially improves on the known worst-case bound of $\Theta(n^2)$ in general connected temporal graphs. A corresponding walk can be constructed in deterministic polynomial time. The upper bound is complemented by lower bounds of $\Omega(n\log(n))$ when $q$ is constant and $\Omega(qn)$ when $1 \leq q \leq n$. We also apply our techniques to the Temporal Rendezvous Problem (TRP), in which two agents that do not communicate have to meet on a vertex of the temporal graph. Our exploration algorithm yields that, with only polynomial-time computational power, the agents can meet in $O(n\log^3(n))$ time steps, leaving a gap of only $\log^2(n)$ to the known lower bound. Dogeas, Erlebach, Kammer, Meintrup, and Moses Jr. [ICALP'24] have shown an $O(rn^{1+\epsilon})$ bound for TEXP, for every fixed $\epsilon > 0$, where $r$ is the number of orbits, and an $O(n^{1+\epsilon})$ bound for TRP. Both results require superpolynomial computation time. Our contribution improves upon these results in several ways. First, the dependence on $n$ in the upper bounds on the number of time steps is decreased from $n^{1+\epsilon}$ to $n\log^3(n)$ for both TEXP and TRP. Second, for TEXP, we bound the number of time steps linearly by the parameter q, which is efficiently computable and upper bounded by $r$. Third, we provide novel deterministic polynomial-time algorithms for both TEXP and TRP.
item.dc:creator: Frank Kammer, Sandra Kiefer, Johannes Meintrup

item.title: Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries
item.description: arXiv:2411.04115v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the tasks of deterministically condensing and extracting from Online Non-Oblivious Symbol Fixing (oNOSF) sources, a natural model of defective randomness where extraction is impossible in many parameter regimes [AORSV, EUROCRYPT'20]. A $(g,\ell)$-oNOSF source is a sequence of $\ell$ blocks where at least $g$ blocks are good (independent, with min-entropy) and the remaining bad blocks are controlled by an online adversary and can be arbitrarily correlated with prior blocks. Previously, [CGR, FOCS'24] proved impossibility of condensing beyond rate $1/2$ when $g\le 0.5 \ell$ and showed existence of condensers for when $g \ge 0.51\ell$ and $n$ is exponential in $\ell$. In this work, not only do we construct the first explicit condensers matching the existential results of [CGR, FOCS'24], but we make a doubly exponential improvement by handling the case when $g\ge 0.51\ell$ and $n$ is only polylogarithmic in $\ell$. We also obtain a much improved explicit construction for transforming low-entropy oNOSF sources into uniform oNOSF sources. Next, we essentially resolve the question of the existence of condensers for oNOSF sources by showing the existence of condensers even when $n$ is a large enough constant and $\ell$ is growing (provided $g \ge 0.51\ell$). We apply our condensers to collective coin flipping and collective sampling, widely studied problems in fault-tolerant distributed computing, and provide very simple protocols for them. Finally, we study the possibility of extraction from oNOSF sources. For lower bounds, we introduce the notion of online influence - extending the notion of influence of boolean functions - and establish tight bounds that imply extraction lower bounds. We also construct explicit extractors via leader election protocols that beat standard resilient functions [AL, Combinatorica'93].
item.dc:creator: Eshan Chattopadhyay, Mohit Gurumukhani, Noam Ringach, Rocco Servedio

item.title: High Precision Multiplicative-Error Approximation of $\#$SAC$^1$ Functions in Logspace Uniform AC$^1$
item.description: arXiv:2610.25623v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cheng and Wang (CCC' 24) showed that BPL is contained in logspace uniform AC$^1$ (denoted as L-AC$^1$). We upgrade their result by showing that approximations of $\#$SAC$^1$ functions can be computed in L-AC$^1$ with multiplicative error $2^{-\mathrm{poly}\log n}$. Previously, approximations of $\#$SAC$^1$ functions are known to be in $\mathsf{NC}^2$ via its exact computation given by Vinay (CCC' 91). A main corollary of our result is that Probabilisitic polynomial time logspace AuxPDMs and Read-$k$ logspace PTMs are computable by L-AC$^1$ with multiplicative error $2^{-\mathrm{poly}\log n}$. Notice that multiplicative error approximations are stronger than additive error approximations in the sense that they can be used to decide both non-deterministic computations and two-sided error probabilistic computations. We note that recently OpenAI announced that BPL $=$ L. Even if we only consider derandomizing probabilistic logspace, our L-AC$^1$ computation has the advantage that the error can be $2^{-\mathrm{poly}\log n}$ and can be multiplicative.
item.dc:creator: Kuan Cheng, Shengtang Huang, Ruiyang Wu

item.title: Supermodular Rank: Set Function Decomposition and Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2305.14632v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We define the supermodular rank of a function on a lattice. This is the smallest number of terms needed to decompose it into a sum of supermodular functions. The supermodular summands are defined with respect to different partial orders. We characterize the maximum possible value of the supermodular rank and describe the functions with fixed supermodular rank. We analogously define the submodular rank. We use submodular decompositions to optimize set functions. Given a bound on the submodular rank of a set function, we formulate an algorithm that splits an optimization problem into submodular subproblems. We show that this method improves the approximation ratio guarantees of several algorithms for monotone set function maximization and ratio of set functions minimization, at a computation overhead that depends on the submodular rank.
item.dc:creator: Rishi Sonthalia, Anna Seigal, Guido Montufar

item.title: Graph-Theoretic Formulation of Hamiltonian and Ground-State Sign Structures in Heisenberg Antiferromagnets
item.description: arXiv:2602.04943v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study Heisenberg antiferromagnets through a graph-theoretic representation of their Hamiltonians. In the computational basis of a fixed-magnetization sector, the Heisenberg Hamiltonian equals a constant minus the weighted Laplacian of a graph whose vertices are spin configurations and whose edges connect configurations related by exchanging two antiparallel spins on a lattice bond. We call this graph the Hilbert graph (HG) which is isomorphic to the token graph of the lattice over which the Hamiltonian is defined. The exact ground-state energy is then determined by the largest eigenvalue of the HG Laplacian, which is the spectral relaxation of weighted Max-Cut on the HG. With the amplitudes fixed, the phase-dependent part of the variational energy defines an antiferromagnetic classical XY model on the HG, with couplings set by the amplitudes. Restricting the variational state to be real, i.e., restricting its phases to $\{0,\pi\}$, reduces the fixed-amplitude energy minimization to solving an antiferromagnetic Ising model and hence a weighted Max-Cut on the HG. When the weights are generated from non-degenerate ground-state amplitudes, the optimal phases give the ground-state sign structure which can be recovered from the weights in time polynomial in the size of the HG. On the Hamiltonian side, a diagonal sign transformation removes all positive off-diagonal matrix elements if and only if the HG is bipartite, which reproduces the Marshall sign rule on bipartite lattices through the graph two-coloring problem; otherwise, the minimal remaining positive weight equals the sum of HG edge weights left uncut by the Max-Cut. This graph formulation establishes a common framework for understanding wave function sign structure, Hamiltonian stoquasticity, non-convexity of phase optimization in variational Monte Carlo, and the average sign in quantum Monte Carlo.
item.dc:creator: Mahmud Ashraf Shamim, Md Moshiur Rahman Raj, Mohamed Hibat-Allah, Ruy Fabila-Monroy, Nobuchika Okada, Paulo T. Araujo

item.title: On the Expressive Power and Limitations of Multi-Layer SSMs
item.description: arXiv:2604.14501v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study how depth, finite precision, state dimension, and chain-of-thought (CoT) affect the expressive power of multi-layer state-space models (SSMs). For the explicit-table $K$-function-composition problem, a canonical benchmark for sequential information propagation, we prove that any $L$-layer SSM solving $(L+3)$-function composition must satisfy $d^2p=\Omega(N/L^3)$, where $d$ is the state dimension and $p$ is the per-scalar precision. Conversely, $K$-function composition is solved exactly by a $(K+1)$-layer generalized SSM with $d=1$ and $p=\Theta(\log N)$. This gives a worst-case depth hierarchy for this formal problem family. We then distinguish post-input reasoning, in which all thought tokens are generated after the input, from input-interleaved reasoning, in which thought tokens may be inserted while the input stream is being read. Post-input reasoning does not circumvent our communication-based lower-bound pipeline, whereas input-interleaved reasoning admits bidirectional simulations with general deterministic one-pass streaming algorithms at the granularity of persistent memory. Finally, width and precision are not interchangeable under exact step-preserving simulation in the base affine-state model, but become interchangeable through the streaming-memory characterization once input-interleaved reasoning is allowed.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR) and NeurIPS, 2026
item.dc:creator: Nikola Zubi\'c, Qian Li, Yuyi Wang, Davide Scaramuzza

item.title: When Does Tool Use Increase the Expressive Power of Finite-Precision Recurrent Models?
item.description: arXiv:2607.06155v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern sequence models are increasingly deployed as agents that interleave token generation with calls to external tools. We study when such tool access increases computational expressivity. We model any fixed finite-precision recurrent sequence model, including finite-precision state-space models (SSMs) with $B$ bits of internal state, as a deterministic finite-state controller interacting with an oracle through a finite command/observation interface, and establish a separation between the two regimes analyzed. First, every finite-state bounded-interface tool with memory set $M$ can be internalized at a cost of at most $\lceil\log_2|M|\rceil+O(1)$ recurrent bits, so the combined system remains finite-state. Second, a single unbounded tape with only local $\mathtt{read}$/$\mathtt{write}$/$\mathtt{move}$ commands suffices for Turing completeness: every single-tape Turing machine with state set $Q$ and tape alphabet $\Gamma$ is simulated by a controller with $O(\log|Q|+\log|\Gamma|)$ recurrent bits, and $\mathrm{EQ}_n$ requires $2^n$ states without tools but one constant-size controller with the tape. Third, this construction is realized exactly by a one-layer finite-precision \emph{selective} affine SSM with binary one-hot states, $\{0,1\}$ transition matrices, and zero biases. Under explicitly stated resource conventions, $O(\log B)$ recurrent bits suffice for tape-assisted simulation of any $B$-state Turing machine, whereas directly realizing an arbitrary $B$-state transition map in one exact affine update without external memory requires total recurrent dimension exactly $B-1$. Fixed description size, occupied tape cells, and interaction cost are reported separately from recurrent memory. Our results concern exact expressivity under deterministic semantics, not learnability or empirical performance.
item.dc:creator: Nikola Zubi\'c, Qian Li, Yuyi Wang, Davide Scaramuzza

item.title: Fixed Sets and the Hardness of Computing Correlated Equilibria
item.description: arXiv:2610.28141v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that computing an approximate correlated equilibrium of a polytope game is PPAD-complete, and thus polynomial-time equivalent to finding a Nash equilibrium. This challenges the conventional view in game theory that correlated equilibria are more tractable objects than Nash equilibria. From a conceptual standpoint, we connect correlated equilibria to a natural generalization of fixed points, which we call fixed sets. A fixed set of a continuous function $f$ is a nonempty finite set $S$ such that $S \subseteq \operatorname{conv} f(S)$. Our main technical contribution is to prove that computing a fixed set is PPAD-hard even at inverse polynomial precision.
item.dc:creator: Ioannis Anagnostides, Constantinos Daskalakis, Gabriele Farina, Noah Golowich, Tuomas Sandholm, Brian Hu Zhang

item.title: Hidden parabolic subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ over finite chain rings
item.description: arXiv:2610.28368v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We give a bounded-error quantum polynomial-time algorithm for finding hidden parabolic subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ over any effectively presented finite chain ring $R$. We call auxiliary group elements or subgroups used to extract information through oracle queries \emph{probes}. For chain length at least two, elementary abelian socle probes first recover the complete flag modulo the maximal ideal. When the residue field has size $q\ge3$, we reconstruct the flag recursively, lifting rank-one terminal members one digit at a time. The intermediate digits reduce to abelian hidden subgroup problems, while the final digit is a finite-field multiple-shift problem solved using learning from subset and Fourier sampling. For $q=2$, where distinct flags can have the same stabilizer, we instead lift the conjugate parabolic subgroup through the congruence filtration. A final linear system determines it modulo normalizer directions. The algorithm outputs generators with probability at least $1-\epsilon$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log|R|,\log(1/\epsilon))$. Consequences include $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})$ for every $N\ge2$ and, with an explicit maximal-order presentation, $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal{O}_K/N\mathcal{O}_K)$ for number fields $K$.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Imran
